claim: MMR-deficient tumors exhibit a hypermutator phenotype with approximately 50 times more novel somatic mutations than MMR-proficient tumors.
source: Application of a standard annotation and filtering pipeline, as previously described (Reumers et al., 2011), revealed that each MMR-deficient tumor exhibited a clear hypermutator phenotype, containing on average 50 times more novel somatic mutations than MMR-proficient tumors (Figure 1A, Figure 1—source data 1, Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by data from whole-genome sequencing analysis and shown in Figure 1A comparing mutation frequencies between MMR-deficient and MMR-proficient tumors.

claim: Orthogonal technologies validated 98% of substitutions and 88% of indels in the three MMR-deficient tumors.
source: Orthogonal technologies validated 98% of substitutions and 88% of indels in the three MMR-deficient tumors, while only 62% of substitutions and 11% of indels were validated in the two MMR-proficient tumors (Figure 1—source data 3).
evidence: Supported by validation experiments using Sequenom MassARRAY genotyping as described in the methods and detailed in Figure 1—source data 3.

claim: All tumors were negative for POLE mutations.
source: Notably, all tumors were negative for POLE mutations (Kandoth et al., 2013; Palles et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by mutation analysis of the sequenced tumors, with reference to prior studies on POLE mutations.

claim: Indels were more frequent than single basepair substitutions in all three MMR-deficient tumors.
source: We observed that indels were indeed more frequent than single basepair substitutions in all three MMR-deficient tumors (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by mutation frequency data shown in Figure 1A comparing indels and substitutions in MMR-deficient tumors.

claim: Indels predominantly affected homopolymers with 40-fold enrichment over expected by chance.
source: Indels predominantly affected homopolymers (40-fold enrichment over expected by chance) and to a lesser extent also microsatellites (2.3-fold enrichment; Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by enrichment analysis comparing observed versus expected indel frequencies in different genomic regions, shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Indels were 91% less frequent in exons compared to other genomic regions.
source: This decrease was caused by indels that were 91% less frequent in exons (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: Supported by mutation frequency analysis stratified by genomic region, shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: 92% of exonic indels resulted in frameshift mutations.
source: Since 92% of exonic indels resulted in frameshift mutations, which have a greater functional impact than substitutions (Montgomery et al., 2013), this suggests that exonic indels are prone to negative clonal selection during tumorigenesis.
evidence: Supported by analysis of indel consequences in exonic regions, with reference to prior work on functional impact of frameshift mutations.

claim: 74% of all substitutions in MMR-deficient tumors represent transitions, similar to patterns observed in matched germ-line.
source: When assessing somatic substitutions in MMR-deficient tumors, we observed that 74% of all substitutions represent transitions (i.e., purine-to-purine or pyrimidine-to-pyrimidine substitutions), which is similar to the patterns observed in the matched germ-line of these tumors (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by substitution pattern analysis comparing MMR-deficient tumors to germ-line DNA, shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Substitution patterns in MMR-deficient tumors are distinct from other tumor genomes including UV-light-induced melanoma, tobacco smoke-induced small cell lung adenocarcinoma, BRCA1-deficient breast tumors, and MMR-proficient endometrial tumors.
source: Indeed, when extending these analyses to other hypermutators, that is, UV-light-induced melanoma (Pleasance et al., 2010), tobacco smoke-induced small cell lung adenocarcinoma (SCLC) (Pleasance et al., 2010), as well as breast tumors deficient for BRCA1 (Nik-Zainal et al., 2012) or EM tumors proficient for MMR, patterns were clearly dissimilar from the matched germ-line (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by comparative analysis of substitution patterns across different tumor types, shown in Figure 2A, with references to prior sequencing studies.

claim: Substitution patterns in MMR-deficient tumors correlate strongly with de novo germ-line substitutions, common genetic variation from the 1000 Genomes Project, and substitutions from human-chimpanzee divergence.
source: On the other hand, de novo germ-line substitutions identified through whole-genome sequencing of parent–offspring trios (Campbell et al., 2012; Kong et al., 2012), common genetic variation as catalogued by the 1000 Genomes Project (1 KG) (1000 Genomes Project Consortium, 2012), and substitutions that occurred in the human lineage during the divergence of humans and chimpanzees correlated strongly to the MMR-deficient tumor genome (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis comparing substitution patterns between MMR-deficient tumors and various germ-line genetic variation datasets, shown in Figure 2A, with references to prior studies.

claim: A considerable fraction of human genetic diversity arises through mismatches escaping MMR.
source: Given these remarkable parallels, we hypothesized that MMR-deficient genomes hypermutate in a way that mirrors the processes driving genetic variation on a population level, albeit somatically and on a shorter time scale.
evidence: Inferred from the strong correlation between MMR-deficient tumor substitution patterns and germ-line genetic variation patterns.

claim: The patterns of all four sets of germ-line genetic variants were highly correlated to MMR-deficient tumors (average R2 = 0.77) at the dinucleotide level.
source: At the small-scale level, when assessing the effect of flanking nucleotides on substitution frequencies, the patterns of all four sets of germ-line genetic variants were highly correlated to MMR-deficient tumors (average R2 = 0.77), but less to the four other cancer genomes (average R2 = 0.45; Figure 2B,C), providing further support for our hypothesis.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of dinucleotide substitution patterns shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: The number of intergenic substitutions per 1 Mb in germ-line genetic variability databases was highly correlated to those in MMR-deficient genomes (average R2 = 0.67).
source: On a large-scale context, the number of intergenic substitutions per 1 Mb in germ-line genetic variability databases was similarly highly correlated to those in MMR-deficient genomes (average R2 = 0.67), but not to those in other cancer genomes (average R2 = 0.42; Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by large-scale correlation analysis shown in Figure 2D comparing substitution distributions across 1 Mb windows.

claim: Six genomic features independently correlated with substitution rates in MMR-deficient tumors as well as with germ-line substitutions.
source: Linear modeling revealed that six of these independently correlated with substitution rates in MMR-deficient tumors as well as with germ-line substitutions (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by multivariate linear regression modeling results shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Replication timing correlated with transitions but not transversions in all three MMR-deficient tumors.
source: First, replication timing correlated with transitions but not transversions in all three MMR-deficient tumors (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by analysis of mutation frequencies binned by replication timing shown in Figure 2F, with statistical significance testing.

claim: The increase in late S phase transversions observed in other genomes contrasts with MMR-deficient tumors where no such increase was observed.
source: This contrasts with the increase in late S phase transversions observed in all other genomes studied here (Figure 2F), as well as in lymphoblastoid cell lines (Koren et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by comparative analysis of replication timing effects shown in Figure 2F, with reference to prior work in lymphoblastoid cell lines.

claim: The absence of increased transversions in late S phase in MMR-deficient cells suggests a reduced fidelity of DNA repair in late S phase in MMR-proficient but not MMR-deficient cells.
source: The increase in MMR-proficient but not MMR-deficient cells suggests a reduced fidelity of DNA repair in late S phase, leading to an increase in transversions. Potential causes include a decreased MMR-activity in late S phase, or a longer window of time available for the repair of early vs late transversions in MMR-proficient cells (Hombauer et al., 2011).
evidence: Inferred from the differential replication timing effects between MMR-proficient and MMR-deficient cells, with reference to prior mechanistic studies.

claim: A 1.6-fold increase in substitutions at bases immediately flanking simple repeats was noted, with a threefold increase next to homopolymers.
source: Indeed, a 1.6-fold increase in substitutions at bases immediately flanking simple repeats was noted, with a threefold increase next to homopolymers and a 1.3-fold increase next to microsatellites (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by analysis of substitution frequencies near repeat regions shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Substitutions flanking repeats predominantly converted the base flanking the repeat to the base constituting the repeat, likely resulting from polymerase slippage events.
source: These substitutions for the vast majority converted the base flanking the repeat, to the base constituting the repeat (Figure 2G). They are thus probably the result of polymerase slippage events, following a mechanism akin to the previously described bacterial dislocation mutagenesis (Kunkel and Soni, 1988).
evidence: Supported by analysis of substitution patterns near homopolymers shown in Figure 2G, with inference about mechanism based on similarity to known bacterial processes.

claim: G:C>A:T transitions in CpG sites strongly depend on CpG content but are inversely correlated with the fraction of CpG islands.
source: Thirdly, G:C>A:T transitions in CpG sites strongly depend on CpG content, but are inversely correlated with the fraction of CpG islands (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by multivariate linear regression modeling results shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The much larger increase in CG>TG transitions observed in MMR-deficient compared to MMR-proficient tumors (3449 vs 145) demonstrates that replication-independent MMR is involved in deamination repair in vivo.
source: Here, the much larger increase in CG>TG transitions observed in MMR-deficient compared to MMR-proficient tumors (3449 vs 145) demonstrates that replication-independent MMR, recently described at the molecular level (Shell et al., 2007; Pena-Diaz et al., 2012), is also involved in deamination repair in vivo (Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by comparison of CG>TG transition frequencies between MMR-deficient and MMR-proficient tumors, with references to prior molecular studies and in vivo work.

claim: Bases outside CpG islands were nearly two times more likely to undergo mutation than those inside CpG islands.
source: Indeed, irrespective of dinucleotide context, bases outside CpG islands were nearly two times more likely to undergo mutation than those inside CpG islands (Figure 2H).
evidence: Supported by analysis of substitution frequencies inside versus outside CpG islands shown in Figure 2H.

claim: DNA methylation appears to contribute to the mutagenic process in MMR-deficient tumors.
source: As CpG islands are generally unmethylated, DNA methylation thus appears to contribute to the mutagenic process. Explanations for this observation include the polymerase stalling that DNA methylation may induce (Song et al., 2012), and the repair of spontaneously deaminated methyl-Cs, which is error-prone and thus mutagenic on its own (Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: Inferred from the differential mutation rates inside versus outside CpG islands, with references to prior mechanistic studies on methylation effects.

claim: Deletions were remarkably more frequent than insertions (81% vs 19%) in MMR-deficient tumors.
source: As observed in other MMR-deficient tumors and also in MMR-deficient Caenorhabditis elegans (Denver et al., 2005; Kim et al., 2013), deletions were remarkably more frequent than insertions (81% vs 19%), confirming that DNA polymerases are more prone to remove than to add a base during DNA synthesis.
evidence: Supported by indel composition analysis with references to prior observations in other MMR-deficient systems.

claim: C:G homopolymers are less likely to accumulate indels compared to A:T homopolymers in MMR-deficient tumors.
source: Although the minority of homopolymers consists of C or G bases (7%), an even smaller fraction of indels affected C:G homopolymers (1.9%; Figure 3C), suggesting that C:G homopolymers are less likely to accumulate indels.
evidence: Supported by analysis of indel distribution across homopolymers of different nucleotide composition shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Each MMR-deficient tumor contained approximately 2015 somatic events versus 39 for MMR-proficient tumors (52-fold increase) in exome sequencing.
source: Exome-sequencing of tumor and matched germ-line DNA at an average coverage of 44x revealed that each MMR-deficient tumor contained ∼2015 somatic events vs 39 for MMR-proficient tumors (52-fold increase; Figure 4A, Figure 4—source data 1, Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by exome sequencing data comparing mutation frequencies between MMR-deficient and MMR-proficient tumors, shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Validation rates for substitutions and indels in exome-sequenced samples were respectively 87% and 86%.
source: Validation rates for substitutions and indels were respectively 87% and 86%.
evidence: Supported by validation experiments on exome-sequenced mutations.

claim: 1.6% of homopolymers was recurrently affected by an indel in the 16 MMR-deficient tumors.
source: Remarkably, 1.6% of homopolymers was recurrently affected by an indel in the 16 MMR-deficient tumors that underwent whole-genome or exome sequencing (i.e., 2244 out of 29,663 homopolymers were affected at least once, whereas 477 were affected at least twice; Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by analysis of recurrent indels across 16 MMR-deficient tumors, with details in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: 34 and 10 homopolymers were affected in ≥6 or ≥8 tumors respectively.
source: Furthermore, 34 and 10 homopolymers were affected in ≥6 or ≥8 tumors (Figure 4—source data 3).
evidence: Supported by recurrent indel analysis data provided in Figure 4—source data 3.

claim: Only 55 substitutions were recurrent, three of which were found in ≥2 tumors.
source: In contrast, only 55 substitutions were recurrent, three of which were found in ≥2 tumors (i.e., two substitutions affecting KRAS codon 12 and 13 were found in three and four tumors [Tie et al., 2011], whereas a substitution in ZNF648 affected three tumors).
evidence: Supported by analysis of recurrent substitutions across the tumor cohort, with reference to prior work on KRAS mutations.

claim: Recurrent indels were more frequently observed than expected based on indel frequency in short, but not in long homopolymers.
source: Remarkably, however, recurrent indels were more frequently observed than expected based on indel frequency in short, but not in long homopolymers (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by enrichment analysis of recurrent indels stratified by homopolymer length, shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Positive clonal selection of indels affecting short homopolymers, which are predominant in coding regions, represents a possible explanation for the enrichment of recurrent indels in short homopolymers.
source: This suggests that features other than homopolymer length underlie indel recurrence rates. Positive clonal selection of indels affecting short homopolymers, which are predominant in coding regions, represents a possible explanation.
evidence: Inferred from the differential enrichment of recurrent indels in short versus long homopolymers and the distribution of homopolymer lengths in coding regions.

claim: The 59-marker panel detected 40 out of 41 tumors MMR-deficient on IHC (sensitivity ~98%) with only 1 out of 184 MMR-normal tumors on IHC identified as MSI (specificity > 99%).
source: At this threshold, our markers detected 40 out of 41 tumors MMR-deficient on IHC (sensitivity ∼98%), while only 1 out of 184 MMR-normal tumors on IHC were identified as MSI (specificity > 99%).
evidence: Supported by validation of the 59-marker panel against IHC results in 236 endometrial tumors.

claim: The 59-marker panel has higher sensitivity compared to the Bethesda panel for detecting MSI in endometrial tumors.
source: However, 12 tumors were positive in the 59-marker panel, but negative in Bethesda. IHC on the nine discordant tumors for which a paraffin block was available confirmed that each of them was MMR-deficient either for MLH1 or MSH2, indicating that the 59-marker panel has a higher sensitivity compared to Bethesda.
evidence: Supported by head-to-head comparison of the 59-marker panel versus Bethesda panel in 114 independent endometrial tumors, with IHC confirmation of discordant cases.

claim: The 59-marker panel correctly identified MSI in colorectal tumors with higher sensitivity than the Bethesda panel.
source: Likewise, we assessed MSI in 126 stage II or III CRC tumors. Each of the 28 MSI tumors on Bethesda was also positive with our 59-marker panel. In contrast, one tumor was MSI-positive in the 59-marker panel but not in the Bethesda panel (Figure 5D). This tumor contained a V600E BRAF mutation and was MLH1 hypermethylated, indicating that it was MMR-deficient and that our panel was also more sensitive for CRC (Deng et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by comparison of the 59-marker panel versus Bethesda panel in 126 colorectal tumors, with molecular confirmation of the discordant case, shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The 59-marker panel can detect MSI in ovarian tumors and leukemias.
source: Finally, we also assessed whether our 59-marker panel can detect MSI in other cancer types. In a limited set of ovarian tumors and leukemias, we indeed correctly identified MSI in each of the samples tested (Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by application of the 59-marker panel to ovarian tumors and leukemia samples, with results detailed in Figure 5—source data 2.

claim: The 'Role of BRCA1 in DNA damage response' pathway was ranked as the top enriched pathway in genes affected by somatic indels in MMR-deficient tumors.
source: Pathway analyses using IPA of all genes affected by a somatic indel, excluding the core MMR genes, ranked the 'Role of BRCA1 in DNA damage response' as the top enriched pathway.
evidence: Supported by IPA pathway analysis of genes with somatic indels.

claim: The 'Double-strand break repair by homologous recombination' pathway ranked top in IPA analysis of genes affected by recurrent indels.
source: IPA analysis of genes affected by recurrent indels moreover revealed that the 'Double-strand break repair by homologous recombination' pathway (DSBR by HR) ranked top (Table 2).
evidence: Supported by IPA pathway analysis of genes with recurrent indels, with results shown in Table 2.

claim: GenomeMuSiC analyses ranked the 'ATR/BRCA pathway' first using BioCarta database and 'DNA repair' pathway first using Reactome database.
source: GenomeMuSiC analyses based on either the independently assembled Reactome or BioCarta pathway databases, ranked respectively the 'ATR/BRCA pathway and the DNA repair' pathway first, with the more specific 'Homologous recombination repair' pathway ranking third in the latter (Table 2).
evidence: Supported by GenomeMuSiC pathway analysis using multiple pathway databases, with results shown in Table 2.

claim: 'Homologous recombination' represented the only DNA repair pathway that was significantly enriched in indels based on the DNARepairDB database.
source: Based on an expert curated DNA repair database (DNARepairDB), 'Homologous recombination' represented the only DNA repair pathway that was significantly enriched in indels.
evidence: Supported by GenomeMuSiC pathway analysis using the DNARepairDB database.

claim: Each MMR-deficient tumor on average contained 3.3 ± 0.4 indels in the 'DSBR by HR' pathway.
source: Since each pathway database differed with respect to the genes included, we finally compiled a literature-based set of genes with proven involvement in DSBR by HR, allowing us to more accurately estimate that each MMR-deficient tumor on average contained 3.3 ± 0.4 indels in the 'DSBR by HR' pathway (Table 2, Table 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by analysis using a custom-defined DSBR by HR pathway based on literature, with results shown in Table 2.

claim: None of the top-ranking pathways contained significantly more homopolymers in their genes than expected.
source: Notably, none of the top-ranking pathways for any of the databases contained significantly more homopolymers in their genes than expected.
evidence: Supported by analysis of homopolymer content in genes within enriched pathways.

claim: The Role of BRCA1 in DNA damage response was amongst the top enriched pathways in TCGA CRC and EM tumor datasets with MSI.
source: IPA analysis confirmed that the Role of BRCA1 in DNA damage response was again amongst the top enriched pathways for each of the data sets. The corresponding p-values were 9.06E−3 and 2.97E−4, although only the latter survived multiple testing correction (p = 0.022; Table 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by IPA pathway analysis of TCGA mutation data from 27 CRC and 65 EM tumors with MSI.

claim: Indels affecting the DSBR by HR pathway were located in the major tumor subclone.
source: First, we confirmed that indels affecting the DSBR by HR pathway were located in the major tumor subclone (Table 2, Table 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by analysis of allelic frequencies of mutations in HR genes, detailed in Table 2—source data 1.

claim: RAD51 foci formation was far less pronounced in MMR-deficient cultures compared to MMR-proficient cultures after exposure to olaparib (p = 0.021) or mitomycin C (p = 0.006).
source: In contrast, although RAD51 foci formation was evident in MMR-deficient and MMR-proficient cultures, the increase was far less pronounced in MMR-deficient cultures (Figure 6A,B), and this for both olaparib (p = 0.021) and mitomycin C (p = 0.006) exposure.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence quantification of RAD51 foci in primary tumor cultures exposed to DSB inducers, shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: The reduction in RAD51 foci in MMR-deficient cells could not be ascribed to differences in RAD51 protein expression or differences in cell cycle between MMR-deficient and -proficient cells.
source: The reduction in RAD51 foci could not be ascribed to differences in RAD51 protein expression or differences in cell cycle between MMR-deficient and -proficient cells, as these were similar between both sets of cultures, under both treated and untreated conditions (Figure 6—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: Supported by cell cycle analysis and protein expression data shown in Figure 6—figure supplements 1–3.

claim: The accumulation of indels in MMR-deficient tumors gradually impairs the DSBR by HR pathway to a level that is intermediate to that of cells heterozygous- and homozygous-deficient for BRCA1.
source: Since RAD51 foci are completely absent upon PARP inhibition in cells with homozygous loss of BRCA1, but not affected in heterozygous mutation carriers (Farmer et al., 2005), these ex vivo data suggest that the accumulation of indels in MMR-deficient tumors gradually impairs the DSBR by HR pathway to a level that is intermediate to that of cells heterozygous- and homozygous-deficient for BRCA1.
evidence: Inferred from the partial reduction in RAD51 foci formation in MMR-deficient cells compared to complete absence in BRCA1 homozygous-deficient cells, with reference to prior work.

claim: MMR-deficient cultures exhibited a dose-dependent decrease in proliferation upon exposure to olaparib, whereas MMR-proficient cultures were only affected at higher concentrations.
source: This revealed that MMR-deficient cultures exhibited a dose-dependent decrease in proliferation upon exposure to olaparib, whereas MMR-proficient cultures were only affected at higher concentrations.
evidence: Supported by dosimetry experiments measuring cell proliferation in response to olaparib.

claim: Cell cytotoxicity assays revealed a dose-dependent sensitivity of MMR-deficient cells to olaparib with 50% growth inhibition (GI50) reached at 26 µM versus 129 µM for MMR-proficient cells (p = 0.0064).
source: Likewise, cell cytotoxicity assays revealed a dose-dependent sensitivity of MMR-deficient cells to olaparib that was more pronounced than in MMR-proficient cells (50% growth inhibition [GI50]) was reached at 26 µM vs 129 µM, respectively, p = 0.0064 (Figure 7A,B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by sulforhodamine B cytotoxicity assays comparing MMR-deficient and MMR-proficient cultures, shown in Figure 7A and 7B.

claim: Mitomycin C and ionizing radiation proved more detrimental for MMR-deficient than MMR-proficient cells.
source: Other DSB-inducing compounds such as mitomycin C or ionizing radiation similarly proved more detrimental for MMR-deficient than MMR-proficient cells (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by cytotoxicity assays comparing sensitivity to mitomycin C and ionizing radiation between MMR-deficient and MMR-proficient cultures, shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Cytotoxicities of paclitaxel were comparable between MMR-deficient and MMR-proficient cells.
source: In contrast, cytotoxicities of other chemotherapeutic compounds such as paclitaxel were comparable between both groups.
evidence: Supported by cytotoxicity assays showing no significant difference in paclitaxel sensitivity between MMR-deficient and MMR-proficient cultures.

claim: A growth inhibition of 50% was reached in MCF7 cells when applying 5.9 nM ATR, 0.88 nM BRCA1 or 0.41 nM BRCA2 siRNA, corresponding respectively to a reduction in expression of 69.5 ± 1.1%, 76.1 ± 4.4%, and 80.0 ± 2.4%.
source: A growth inhibition of 50% was reached in MCF7 cells when applying 5.9 nM ATR, 0.88 nM BRCA1 or 0.41 nM BRCA2 siRNA, corresponding respectively to a reduction in expression of 69.5 ± 1.1%, 76.1 ± 4.4%, and 80.0 ± 2.4% (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by siRNA knockdown experiments in MCF7 cells measuring olaparib sensitivity and gene expression levels, shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The loss of DSBR by HR activity in MMR-deficient tumors corresponds to a loss of about 75–80% BRCA1 or BRCA2 expression.
source: These data thus suggest that the loss of DSBR by HR activity in MMR-deficient tumors corresponds to a loss of about 75–80% BRCA1 or BRCA2 expression.
evidence: Inferred from the siRNA knockdown experiments showing that 75-80% reduction in BRCA1 or BRCA2 expression produces similar olaparib sensitivity as observed in MMR-deficient tumors.

claim: Lynch syndrome is responsible for 2–5% of endometrial or colorectal tumors.
source: Lynch syndrome is responsible for 2–5% of endometrial (EM) or colorectal (CRC) tumors.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about Lynch syndrome prevalence.

claim: Epigenetic silencing of MLH1 contributes to another 15–28% of endometrial or colorectal tumors.
source: Additionally, epigenetic silencing of MLH1 contributes to another 15–28% of these tumors (Parsons et al., 2012; Peltomaki, 2014).
evidence: Statement of established knowledge with references to prior studies.

claim: Deficiency of the MMR machinery leads to DNA replication errors in the tumor tissue, but not the normal surrounding tissue.
source: Deficiency of the MMR machinery leads to DNA replication errors in the tumor tissue, but not the normal surrounding tissue.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about MMR deficiency effects.

claim: Errors often accumulate as indel mutations in mono- and di-nucleotide repeats—a phenomenon referred to as microsatellite instability (MSI).
source: In particular, errors often accumulate as indel mutations in mono- and di-nucleotide repeats—a phenomenon referred to as microsatellite instability (MSI) (Pinol et al., 2005).
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about MSI with reference to prior work.

claim: Untreated CRC patients with MMR-deficient tumors have a modestly better prognosis, but do not seem to benefit from 5-fluorouracil-based adjuvant chemotherapy.
source: Untreated CRC patients with MMR-deficient tumors have a modestly better prognosis, but do not seem to benefit from 5-fluorouracil-based adjuvant chemotherapy, which is the first-choice chemotherapy for CRC.
evidence: Statement of established clinical knowledge about MMR-deficient tumor prognosis and treatment response.

claim: In MMR-deficient tumors, mismatches induced by 5-fluorouracil are tolerated, leading to failure to induce cell death.
source: In particular, in MMR-deficient tumors, mismatches induced by 5-fluorouracil are tolerated, leading to failure to induce cell death (Fischer et al., 2007).
evidence: Statement of established mechanism with reference to prior work.

claim: MMR-deficient tumors are resistant to cisplatin and carboplatin, which are frequently used chemotherapies in EM cancer.
source: MMR-deficient tumors are also resistant to cisplatin and carboplatin, which are frequently used chemotherapies in EM cancer (Hewish et al., 2010).
evidence: Statement of established clinical knowledge with reference to prior work.

claim: MMR-deficient tumors can acquire resistance to targeted therapies through secondary mutations in genes that activate alternative or downstream signaling pathways.
source: Furthermore, MMR-deficient tumors can be resistant to targeted therapies, because they acquire secondary mutations in genes that activate alternative or downstream signaling pathways (e.g., PIK3CA).
evidence: Statement of established mechanism of resistance in MMR-deficient tumors.

claim: Epigenetic silencing of MLH1 coincides with the BRAF V600E mutation, which represents an established negative predictor of response to targeted anti-EGFR therapies in advanced CRC.
source: Another possibility is that epigenetic silencing of MLH1 coincides with particular mutations, such as the BRAF V600E mutation (Donehower et al., 2013), which represents an established negative predictor of response to targeted anti-EGFR therapies in advanced CRC (Richman et al., 2009).
evidence: Statement of established clinical knowledge with references to prior studies.

claim: Increased oxidative damage and interference with the base excision repair pathway can sensitize MMR-deficient tumors.
source: In particular, increased oxidative damage (by methotrexate exposure or PINK1 silencing [Martin et al., 2011]) and interference with the base excision repair (BER) pathway (by DNA polymerase γ or β inhibition [Martin et al., 2010]) can sensitize MMR-deficient tumors.
evidence: Statement of prior research findings with references to specific studies.

claim: Findings on synthetic lethal interactions within the MMR pathway have failed to translate into clinically effective treatment options.
source: Until now, these findings failed, however, to translate into clinically effective treatment options.
evidence: Statement about the clinical translation status of prior research.

claim: The first whole-exome sequencing of MMR-deficient tumors highlighted the clearly distinct mutational landscape of these tumors.
source: More recently, the first whole-exome sequencing of MMR-deficient tumors was performed, highlighting the clearly distinct mutational landscape of these tumors (TCGA, 2012), whereas at the whole-genome level, Kim et al. (2013) revealed overrepresentation of MSI in euchromatic and intronic regions compared to heterochromatic and intergenic regions.
evidence: Statement of prior research findings with references to TCGA and Kim et al. studies.
